newsitem.title: USA: U.S. producer prices' December gain biggest of 1996.
newsitem.headline: U.S. producer prices' December gain biggest of 1996.

text.p: Prices at the wholesale level posted their biggest increase all year in December, the government said Thursday, as surging energy prices jolted an an otherwise calm inflation report.
The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index rose 0.5 percent last month, the biggest monthly increase since December 1995's gain of 0.6 percent. The index rose 0.4 percent in November.

But excluding food and energy prices, the "core" rate of inflation rose by a scant 0.1 percent in December, matching November's rise. That helped ease investors' fears of a pickup in inflation and sparked a rally in the bond market that spilled over into stocks.
"Going forward, it looks like inflation is very well contained," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
But another economist predicted that the spike in energy prices could continue to bedevil the inflation outlook.
"We should expect to see energy-consuming companies attempting to restore diminished profit margins by lifting product prices," said Ken Maynard, chief economist at KeyCorp in Cleveland.

Still, with inflation concentrated in the energy sector, the Federal Reserve is "likely to practice forbearance for a while longer," Maynard said. The central bank has held rates steady since cutting them last January.
Wall Street economists had forecast a 0.3 percent rise in wholesale prices overall and a 0.1 percent rise in the core rate.

The 30-year Treasury bond rose more than a point after the report, driving its yield down to 6.75 percent from 6.84 percent on Wednesday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction. Inflation is a bond investor's worst enemy as it erodes the returns on long-term investments.

The drop in long-term interest rates sparked a rally in the stock market, and the Dow Jones industrial average rose 76.19 points to 6,625.67, according to preliminary tallies, its third record in four sessions.

For all of 1996, producer prices rose 2.8 percent compared to 2.3 percent in 1995. But excluding the volatile food and energy components, prices rose only 0.6 percent last year, the second smallest gain on record.
Energy prices jumped 3.1 percent in December, the biggest increase since December 1995's 3.8 percent gain.
Natural gas prices climbed 1.7 percent after rising a record 3.8 percent in November. Gasoline prices surged 5.2 percent in December while heating oil prices rose 4.9 percent.

Food prices fell 0.1 percent last month, matching November's drop. They had been expected to fall more than they did, which helps explain why forecasters had been calling for a smaller gain in the overall PPI.
Passenger car prices rose 0.3 percent in December following a gain of 0.5 percent in November. Tobacco prices rose 0.3 percent after rising 0.1 percent in November.
In December, prices of intermediate goods -- those that require further processing -- rose 0.4 percent after gaining 0.2 percent the previous month.
Prices of crude goods jumped 4.2 percent after rising 1.8 percent in November. But after subtracting food and energy's impact, crude goods prices rose just 0.2 percent.
In another report, the department said first-time jobless claims fell 13,000 to 361,000 in the week ended Jan. 4 from a revised 374,000 the prior week.
The less volatile four-week moving average rose to 357,250 from 354,500.
